One dead in new attack on Saudi airport, a day after Houthi strike kills 13

Saudi-led coalition forces in Yemen said an unidentified projectile had targeted Riyadh's international airport Terminal 4 on Sunday, causing a fire. Eleven people were wounded in addition to the fatality, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.

RIYADH: One person was killed and nearly a dozen hurt in a new attack on Riyadh's international airport on Sunday (Oct 11), Saudi authorities reported, a day after a strike claimed by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300. Saudi-led coalition forces in Yemen said an unidentified projectile had targeted Riyadh's international airport Terminal 4 on Sunday, causing a fire. Eleven people were wounded in addition to the fatality, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. Coalition forces also said Saudi air defences had intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of King Khalid International Airport. They later added that a drone had been intercepted and destroyed in the country's Eastern Province, and a ballistic missile launched towards Khamis Mushait had been intercepted.  Emergency alerts were also issued in Abha, in the south, early on Monday but the danger had since passed, the Saudi Civil Defense said.

The strikes have exposed vulnerabilities in Saudi defence capabilities as the kingdom wages an air campaign against the Houthis, who are fighting a ground war in Yemen against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Footage released by Saudi state television of the Saturday attack on the Riyadh airport showed scores of religious pilgrims lined up at a gate as they prepared to travel to Islam's two holiest sites. A bright orange flash sent people running in panic, while parts of the roof appeared to cave in. The airport was closed after the attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. HOUTHIS CLAIM RESPONSIBILITY FOR OTHER ATTACKS In a televised speech on Sunday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for Saturday's attack and said the group had struck the airport in Dammam in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province and two facilities of Saudi oil giant Saudi Aramco. The Saudi government's media office and Aramco did not respond to requests for comment. The Saudi civil aviation authority confirmed the strike on Dammam's King Fahd International Airport late on Sunday, adding that "damage assessments and safety inspections of airport facilities are under way."

Related:

Saudi Arabia says three killed at airport as Yemen war expands

Singapore condemns Houthi attacks on civilian aviation infrastructure in Saudi Arabia

An eyewitness aboard a taxiing aircraft at Dammam told Reuters that around 8.30pm (1.30am, Monday, Singapore time) on Sunday, they saw a projectile strike the tarmac beside several parked aircraft, causing a fire. The witness said the aircraft returned to the gate. Passengers disembarked and were told to leave. Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 showed several delays and cancellations on Sunday for arrivals and departures at Dammam airport, the kingdom's third-largest. The Houthis earlier on Sunday had renewed their warning against using Saudi airports. "We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions," the group said. Britain's embassy in Saudi Arabia in a post on X advised British citizens against all but essential travel to Jeddah, Dammam and all airports in the kingdom except the airport in Medina. US aviation authorities issued a notice to US airlines to use caution while flying to or over the kingdom. "WORSE IS YET TO COME," HOUTHIS WARN Saudi Arabia has recently stepped up its military involvement in Yemen, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a government counteroffensive after the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month. The Houthis said on Sunday that Saudi Arabia carried out 124 air strikes in Yemen in the past 24 hours. "Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," Yemen's Houthi-run foreign ministry said in statements carried by Al Masirah television. US President Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel launched in February. In a post on Telegram, Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said he told his Saudi counterpart that Tehran was ready to help facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

Related:

Türkiye sending technical, defensive support to Saudi Arabia to help fight Houthis, officials say

ENERGY CONFERENCE STILL GOING AHEAD A five-day conference of international energy organisation WPC Energy opened as planned on Sunday at a convention centre about 10km from the Riyadh airport, the Saudi energy ministry said. A ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum also went ahead, according to a media advisory from the ministry. It was not clear which ministers attended. Italy's energy minister, Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, whose country was co-hosting, had said on Friday he would participate remotely via video link. German officials were trying to organise a return flight for economy minister Katherina Reiche. She was supposed to return to Berlin from Riyadh on Monday but the ministry said it appeared likely her flight would be unable to take off. Separately, Saudi authorities announced that in-person classes at schools in Riyadh would be shifted to remote learning from Sunday until Thursday. Sunday's attack brought the death toll in attacks on Riyadh's airport to 18 for the week. In Saturday's attack, the dead included four Saudis while the remainder were foreign nationals, Saudi authorities said.

Source: Reuters/rk

UK PM Burnham says Russia interfered in 2016 Brexit vote

Russia has previously denied meddling in the Brexit vote, casting Britain as gripped by anti-Russian hysteria.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham gives a television interview following his meeting with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, in Berlin, Germany, on Oct 8, 2026. (File photo: Reuters/Sean Gallup)

FAST

LONDON: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit vote, as he warned voters in France and Germany about Moscow-backed efforts to influence their politics. Burnham, who took over as Britain's leader in July and said last month that Britain could consider rejoining the European Union in the future, is the first British prime minister to say openly there was evidence of Russian interference in the referendum a decade ago. "I asked the question coming to Downing Street, was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? And I've had the clear answer that yes, there was," Burnham said in an interview with The Rest Is Politics podcast released on Sunday (Oct 11). Burnham did not spell out how he believed that Russia interfered in the referendum and gave no details on what evidence this statement was based.

The Russian embassy in London did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Russia has previously denied meddling in the Brexit vote, casting Britain as gripped by anti-Russian hysteria.

Related:

Burnham's comments mark a departure from those of former Prime Minister Boris Johnson, who campaigned to leave the EU, and said in 2020 there was no evidence of Russian interference in the referendum. Britons voted 52 per cent to 48 per cent to leave the EU in 2016, plunging the country into its biggest political crisis since World War II. Burnham said voters in European democracies needed to be better informed about efforts to disrupt their politics. "I mean, these things are important now to put clearly on the record, and I believe, help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia," he said. Britain's government failed to establish whether Russia meddled in the 2016 referendum on membership of the EU, according to a report by parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee in 2020. The report also found that Russia had sought to influence Scotland's 2014 independence referendum, in which voters rejected independence. Burnham last month said he could campaign to take Britain back into the EU at the next general election, reopening the country’s divisive debate on its relationship with the continent.

Source: Reuters/fs

WASHINGTON: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday (Oct 11) in response to critical comments from US President Donald Trump that he will organise elections in Ukraine if Russian President Vladimir Putin agrees to a 60-day ceasefire. "Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organise elections," Zelenskyy told ABC's This Week. Trump on Saturday criticised Zelenskyy for attacking Russian oil refineries a day after the US temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian fuel that were designed to deprive Moscow of revenues to fund its war in Ukraine. "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president," Trump had told reporters at the White House.

He said it is easy for Ukraine to be blamed for higher fuel prices "when everybody in the world understands because of the war in (the) Middle East, the prices are rising."

Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow ceases its own strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Under terms of the deal as described by Trump on Friday, Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets, equal to about 2.25 million barrels of fuel. The US exports about 1.5 million barrels of diesel per day. Trump is under pressure to bring down rising fuel prices ahead of November midterm elections that will determine whether his Republican Party will retain control of the US Congress for his final two years in office. Many lawmakers, including Republicans, have criticised the diesel deal as rewarding Putin.

WARSAW: Polish police have detained a man suspected of planning an attack on Prime Minister Donald Tusk, the Interior Minister said on Sunday (Oct 11), after it warned earlier of a threat to Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz. "The man who threatened and planned an attack on Prime Minister Donald Tusk has been detained by Polish police," Marcin Kierwinski wrote on X, without giving further details. Tusk thanked the police for "swift and decisive action" in a separate post on X. Polish security services earlier convened a special meeting after receiving information about a potential attack, a spokesperson said.

"We are talking about a high probability of these threats being carried out," he told reporters. Interior Ministry Spokesperson Karolina Galecka said an email with information about the potential attack had been forwarded to police by the State Protection Service, which is responsible for ministers' security. While violent crime is relatively rare in Poland, the country is deeply polarised politically and has faced security threats due to its proximity to the war in Ukraine. In August, police detained a 23-year-old man accused of calling for the assassination of senior Polish politicians. VATICAN CITY: Pope Leo said on Sunday (Oct 11) that doctors had detected a small growth on his lung during a recent health check and he would be undergoing surgery this week to remove it, in the first health scare of the 71-year-old pontiff's tenure. Pope Leo told pilgrims in St. Peter's Square for his weekly Sunday prayer that the growth was "well-contained" and had been spotted early. The Vatican did not say whether the nodule is believed to be malignant. "Recently, during some medical examinations, doctors found a localised nodule in my lung," said the pontiff. "It was detected at a very early stage and is well contained."

"The doctors believe it is advisable to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to remove it," he said. "The operation is already scheduled for the next few days." A nodule on the lung is a small, localised lesion that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than 5 per cent of lung nodules overall prove cancerous, although risk rises with age, size and other factors such as smoking. Pope Leo, elected pope by the world's cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to previously have had health issues.

Related:

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wished the pope well. "I would like to express to the Holy Father my personal support, and that of the Italian government, as he faces this challenge in the coming days," she said in a statement. "The serenity and composure with which he spoke about it during today’s Angelus are reassuring," Meloni added. The late Pope Francis, Pope Leo's predecessor, died at age 88 and was increasingly frail in his later years. The Vatican press office said the pope's recovery from surgery was expected to take about a week. It did not immediately provide further details about the pope's health. Pope Leo keeps a busy schedule and is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from Nov 6 to 17. Before mentioning his health issue in his address on Sunday, the pope referred to the trip, thanking Catholics for their prayers "for the pastoral visit I will undertake".

Source: Reuters/fh

Indian capital braces for second day of protests against poll chief

Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel continued to be deployed across New Delhi on Sunday (Oct 11) although metro stations reopened and mobile internet services were back up.

Security personnel are seen at a blocked road amid ongoing protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter roll irregularities, near Jantar Mantar in New Delhi on Oct 11, 2026. (Photo: AFP/Sajjad Hussain)

NEW DELHI: New Delhi braced for a second day of youth protests demanding the resignation of India's election chief on Sunday (Oct 11), as a court ordered the release of "cockroach" movement founder Abhijeet Dipke and two other senior leaders. Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) , and the other leaders were detained when their plane landed in Delhi on Saturday as the movement planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in Central Delhi. They were produced in front of a magistrate early on Sunday. "Condition - no breach of peace for one year," the CJP's legal head Ratna Singh said in a post on X announcing their release.

Activist and social media influencer Dhruv Rathee, who was also among those detained, was released past midnight on condition he did not participate in any further protests, said an interior ministry official who declined to be named.

Related:

Indian police detain Cockroach Janta Party founder ahead of youth protest

India detains thousands, locks down Delhi to foil election chief protest

Police detained more than 2,000 people and locked down Delhi's city centre to thwart Saturday's protest, and thousands of police and paramilitary personnel continued to be deployed across the city on Sunday although metro stations reopened and mobile internet services were back up. Most of those detained on the first day of protests were released late on Saturday night, police said. Opposition parties and critics of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government criticised what they said was the high-handed use of force against the protesters, while a UN body called on authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly was respected and fulfilled. India's foreign ministry said on Sunday the UN's approach was "selective" and its statement constituted "an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India."

A man rides a scooter past shuttered shops in a deserted market, on the second day of a protest by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) seeking the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India on Oct 11, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Bhawika Chhabra)

MILLIONS OF NAMES REMOVED FROM ELECTORAL ROLL The protests are calling for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a revision of voter lists that critics say disproportionately benefits Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which has been in power for more than 12 years. Sporadic protests have been going on across India since the Indian Express newspaper in late September reported Kumar's two deputies raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems. The Commission says differing views are normal in internal deliberations, and has denied favouring any party. Modi's BJP has accused groups opposed to it of trying to undermine the country's democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.

Commuters cross a checkpoint as police officers stand guard on the second day of a protest planned by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) seeking the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India on Oct 11, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Priyanshu Singh)

Election Commission data cited by the party shows about 130 million names, more than the population of Japan, have been deleted from electoral rolls during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated and 30 million who could not be traced. The BJP and the Commission deny allegations of manipulation, although opposition parties say Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately impacted by the deletions. The cockroach party, which began as an online satire, rapidly evolved into a pressure group, with street protests against exam paper leaks culminating in the resignation of Modi's education minister. The CJP has called its protests against Kumar "Season 2" on its social media handles, and said it would not stop until India's election system was reformed.

South Korea completes Arctic-Europe commercial voyage, eyes regular service despite risks

South Korean President President Lee Jae Myung has made Arctic shipping a priority, and officials hope to launch regular services by 2030.

FAST

SEOUL: A South Korean container ship completed the country's first commercial round trip to Europe via the Arctic on Sunday (Oct 11), as authorities bank on the route helping turn the port of Busan into a global maritime hub. The PanStar Acro docked in the southeastern port 50 days after setting sail on Aug 22. Authorities say the Arctic route could cut typical voyage times by around a third. President Lee Jae Myung has made Arctic shipping a priority, and officials hope to launch regular services by 2030. But the project risks friction with Western allies hoping to keep Russia isolated during its war in Ukraine. The route runs along Russia's Arctic coast, and Seoul consulted with Moscow about the journey, including whether the ship needed help to tackle any problems, such as getting stuck in ice. On its outbound voyage, the vessel passed through Arctic waters and reached its first European port, Felixstowe in Britain, before calling at Rotterdam and Gdansk and returning home via the Arctic. The trial voyage also highlighted the challenges ahead. Before the departure, PanStar told Reuters it was seeking about 1,300 twenty-foot equivalent units of cargo, but the ship left with 737 TEU of cargo plus empty containers. Industry experts have said the route's value will depend on reliable schedules, the costs of slowing to avoid ice, special insurance premiums and extra fuel use.

KATHMANDU: Nepali authorities urged villagers on Sunday (Oct 11) to move to safer places after a massive flood in a river in the central part of the country swept away several houses and infrastructure, but there were no reports of any casualties. A dry landslide in Chumnubri village in Gorkha district, about 100km west of Kathmandu, blocked the Budhi Gandaki River, leading to downstream flooding, authorities said. The Budhi Gandaki is a tributary of the Trishuli River, downstream from another tributary where a glacier collapse caused a catastrophic flood in August that killed 1,457 people, with thousands still missing. "We have asked villagers living along the river banks downstream to evacuate and remain safe," said Dharmendra Kumar Mishra, the Gorkha district's most senior bureaucrat.

Mishra said about a dozen houses and two suspension bridges had been swept away, and a hydroelectric project was damaged by the flood. The flooded river carrying muddy sludge is rising and has washed away a highway bridge connecting Gorkha with the neighbouring Dhading district, said Dharam Raj Uprety, chief of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. The army rescued six people from Jagat who were facing the risk of a landslide, Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in a social media post. Another 18 workers at the hydroelectric project that had its camp was damaged escaped to safety, Uprety said. National disaster authorities alerted people living along the river in the Gorkha, Tanahun, Chitwan, East Nawalparasi and West Nawalparasi districts about the flood. "Please help ensure that people in at-risk areas are moved to safe locations in time and assist search and rescue operations as needed," the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said in a social media post. Officials said army and police rescue personnel had reached the area and were also monitoring the situation from a helicopter.

WHO unsure what caused pneumonia that killed plague-lab worker in Russia

The lab worker fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances on Oct 2, prompting authorities to quarantine about 200 people and causing public health fears on social media.

GENEVA: The World Health Organization (WHO) said on Saturday (Oct 10) that it still does not know what caused the pneumonia that killed a Russian lab worker at an anti-plague research centre in Siberia this month, and that no case of plague had been registered. The WHO said the Russian state regulator reported that tests of the lab worker and those who came in contact with her were negative for the high-threat pathogens tested, that her contacts still showed no symptoms, and that no further linked cases of severe pneumonia had been identified. "Based on the information provided ... (the) WHO has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission associated with this event. A key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker," it said in a statement. The lab worker fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances on Oct 2, prompting authorities to quarantine about 200 people and causing public health fears on social media. Global health officials have been extra alert to fatal pneumonia cases of undetermined cause since the COVID-19 pandemic, which began with a cluster of fast-spreading fatal respiratory illness in China. The cause of individual pneumonia cases can often not be determined. Russian authorities have said the lab worker was appropriately vaccinated and that they found no microorganisms linked to her work in her body. On Thursday, Russia said it had completed health checks on all the worker's contacts. It says it had provided full information to the WHO according to established procedures.
